P1.evidence: There was no setter pre-qualification to read back — the prospect arrived through Instagram DMs and did not know whether he had been talking to a person, so P1a does not apply. The rep did try: 'I also want to pull up the notes, because you spoke with, who did you speak with earlier?' The frame was the usual three parts plus next steps: 'get a super crystal clear picture on where you're at in your fitness, where you're looking to get to, what's missing. And then from there, we can kind of look at what a potential game plan could look like for you.' Agreement taken with 'Does that all sound good?' and the open question ran verbatim.

P2.evidence: Age, height, weight and body fat all confirmed. Work asked and explored properly, including the career change out of tech. Training week gathered in detail down to sets, reps and duration. Diet asked and the drinking probed twice, including 'is that the primary reason we're limiting drinking, or is there other reasons?' Results from current training asked with a scale: 'how are we actually feeling about the physique right now as a whole, like one to 10?' — 'maybe like a seven.' Injuries and health conditions asked in a single combined question, which surfaced the back injury; hereditary conditions were never asked. Sitting was never asked. Sleep surfaced only incidentally inside the intermittent-fasting discussion and energy was never asked at all.

P3.evidence: The vision question ran with a useful prompt: 'what would be like the perfect vision for your body? Are we talking like, hey, I want to be like Brad Pitt from Troy?' The reflect-back was the best in the batch and ran twice, both confirmed: 'the workouts we're doing right now sound kind of long and miserable. And we're wanting to find a system that works for us that we can be consistent with and build the habits before having a child in the next year or so. Was that kind of hit the nail on the head?' — 'Yeah, totally.' Then 'it seems like the functional aspect, like injury prevention long-term... Is that kind of what I'm hearing?' — 'Yeah, that's a good distillation.' But the outside-the-physical bridge was never actually asked; the child, the surrogacy and the identity shift were all volunteered. Nothing was asked about who else this impacts until the spouse became a commercial obstacle, and nothing was asked about a physical thing he wants to do and cannot.

P4.evidence: Past attempts fully mapped — Kalos, the DEXA plan, the previous coach Andrew, an earlier period training kettlebells exclusively. What happened was quantified: 17% down to 14% and back to 16%. Why it did not stick was probed at the specific level, not the general one: 'What happened last week?' — 'guests came into town... I don't do so well with consistency when there's chaos.' The gap question ran and produced the most valuable moment on the call, which the prospect explicitly recognised as new to himself: 'I think it's the accountability thing... I am just thinking about this out loud right now and I'll say it for the first time... the accountability thing will be the thing that catapults it into the next level. And so that's kind of like the glass ceiling for me.'

P5.evidence: The two-year question was asked once, in passing, immediately after the prospect's glass-ceiling admission — 'what happens if we just continue just not really being accountable and actually going all in on something, like what happens two years, three years down the road?' — and the prospect answered 'Yeah, totally', which is not an answer. The rep accepted it and moved on. That is the phase's single best opportunity in the batch, arriving one second after the prospect had opened himself up, and it was spent in a sentence. No settling question, no why-not, and the line in the sand was asserted rather than asked: 'we're ready to draw a line of sand and make a change, is that kind of what I'm understanding?'

P6.evidence: The strongest P6 in the batch and run before the price. Belief: 'do you feel like that's everything that you need to not just get in the best shape of your life, but also to learn everything that you need to maintain it well into the future?' — 'Yeah, I feel like that's like, those are the pillars, for sure.' Commitment: 'are you fully committed to really getting the same dial... and really learning these skills so you can have them for the rest of your life?' — 'Yeah, definitely. I feel like it's coming in a timely way right now.' He also re-confirmed belief a third time after the price and got a clean yes. The one weakness is that P6a was framed as a product-fit question rather than a self-belief question, so it tested the offer rather than the man.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and no payment was collected, so step 1 is a miss and steps 2-4 were unreachable. The failure was mechanical rather than commercial: the terms were agreed at two payments of $3,000, the prospect asked three times for an invoice with a secure payment link, and the rep could not supply one and did not commit to producing one. The call ended with the prospect asking the rep to go and find out whether the business can do it.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete play run anywhere in this batch, and close to the scripted order. Money-aside isolation ran: 'finances aside, is there anything else at all that's keeping you from being less than 100% certain that this is the right thing and now's the right time?' Would-the-partner-object ran twice: 'I would assume your partner, is he pretty on board with you getting into really good shape?' and 'what do you think a potential concern he might have?' — answer, only the total investment. Input-versus-permission ran almost verbatim: 'have you already decided you're doing this 100% and you're just letting him know out of respect? Or is it more like, hey, we make all financial decisions together?' Whose-responsibility ran at length via the business analogy — 'why do you feel like it's fair to go to him and ask him to make a decision on something that he doesn't fully know about, and he'll never actually be responsible for the results?' The hypothetical close ran: 'if Ryan was here right now and he was like, Saagar, I'm going to support whatever you want to do... would it be like Michael, here's my credit card?' — 'that's like a pretty fair assessment.' And the fallback deposit ran. One material omission: the script attaches a full refund if the partner says no, and the refund condition was never stated. The prospect also gave a substantive counter the play has no answer for — the money leaves shared accounts, so it is genuinely joint — and he repeated it at the end: 'it's personal investments and making sure that we're aligned on what's literally coming out of our accounts in a given month.'

Trigger was mild and structural rather than about capacity — 'if we're able to break it up a little bit, I think that's a lot more doable than everything up front.' The rep isolated correctly and then conceded the half-half instantly: 'Dude, we can do the half-half. That's not an issue.' No financial-picture questions, which was arguably right for this prospect, but no exchange either — the concession was given away rather than traded for a decision on the call, which was the obvious ask.

Script gap and the reason this call did not close. The prospect refused to read a card number aloud and asked, three separate times, for an invoice with a secure payment link he could document: 'the security of the payment, it would be nice if it was like an invoice or something that I could pay with a link', then 'when you do use an invoice, how do they pay?', then at the very end 'if there's any way to do like a secure payment link to an invoice so that I can document that, that would be ideal.' The rep had no process, questioned the concern — 'is that that we're just going to take your card and run off to Mexico?' — and disclosed that he takes card numbers verbally and enters them into his own processor. The playbook has no payment-method branch at all, and this is a business-owner segment that will routinely want documented, invoiced payment. It cost a deal that was otherwise agreed on terms.

Second gap — an incumbent paid provider whose price was never established. He is switching from Kalos, which bundles DEXA scanning with nutrition and workout coaching, and intends to keep the DEXA portion. The rep never asked what Kalos costs, never positioned against it, and told him the DEXA data would not drive programme changes — 'it's not going to be the DEXA scan that's going to dictate the changes' — which quietly removed the measurement system the prospect trusts most. OC assumes the blocker is capacity; here there was a live competitor sitting unpriced on the table.

notes: Discovery, reflect-back and the commitment check were all run properly and the prospect self-diagnosed his own ceiling out loud — and then the consequence frame was spent in a single unanswered sentence at exactly the moment it would have been worth most. The deal itself was lost on plumbing: terms were agreed and the close failed because the business cannot issue an invoice with a secure payment link. That is fixable this week and worth more than any script change.
